'''Gujarmal Modi'''  (9 August 1902 – 22 January 1976) was an Indian industrialist and philanthropist who co-established the [[Modi Group]] of companies and the industrial city of [[Modinagar]] in 1933, along with his brother Kedar Nath Modi.<ref>{{cite web|last=John|first=Satish|title=After Ambanis, it's Modis' turn to show sibling camaraderie at BK Modi's birthday|url=http://articles.economictimes.indiatimes.com/2012-01-02/news/30587680_1_modi-brothers-modi-group-kk-modi|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120113163526/http://articles.economictimes.indiatimes.com/2012-01-02/news/30587680_1_modi-brothers-modi-group-kk-modi|url-status=dead|archive-date=13 January 2012|publisher=The Economic Times|access-date=24 January 2014}}</ref>{{Failed verification|date=April 2024}} A sugar mill in Modinagar marked the beginning of the Modi Group conglomerate, which later diversified into varied fields.<ref>{{cite web|title=About Gujarmal Modi|url=http://umeshmodigroup.com/About.aspx|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110410123000/http://www.umeshmodigroup.com/About.aspx|url-status=dead|archive-date=10 April 2011|access-date=23 January 2014}}</ref>

GM Modi established schools and colleges at his birthplace, Mahendragarh, in [[Patiala]] and in Modinagar. He also contributed in the field of higher education by giving grants to established institutions such as [[Banaras Hindu University]], and different colleges in [[Meerut]] and other places. He was awarded the [[Padma Bhushan]] by the [[Government of India]] in 1968.<ref>{{cite web|title=Padma Bhushan Awardees|publisher=[[Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (India)|Ministry of Communications and Information Technology]]|url=http://india.gov.in/myindia/padmabhushan_awards_list1.php}}</ref> He is the grandfather of [[Lalit Modi]], the founder of the [[Indian Premier League]] (IPL).<ref name=Forbes>{{cite web|last=Schwartz|first=Peter|title=The World's Hottest Sports League|url=https://www.forbes.com/2009/08/27/cricket-india-ipl-business-sports-ipl.html|work=Forbes|access-date=23 January 2014}}</ref><ref name="The Economic Times">{{cite news|last=Mukherjee|first=Shubham|title=Lalit will head family flagship, says father|url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/lalit-will-head-family-flagship-says-father/articleshow/5862278.cms|newspaper=The Economic Times|date=27 April 2010 |access-date=23 January 2014}}</ref>

==Early life==
Gujarmal Modi was born as Ram Prasad Modi on 9 August 1902, in [[Mahendragarh]] (now in [[Haryana]] state) to a [[Marwari people|Marwari]] Family. He was the second child of his father, Multani Mal Modi, and the only child of his mother, Chandi Devi, who was Multani Mal's second wife. Chandi Devi died of sepsis only six days after the birth of Gujarmal. Multani Mal then married a third time, and it was his step-mother, Gujri Devi, who reared Gujarmal. All his life, Gujarmal was to share a relationship of great affection and attachment with his step-mother. He gave up his real name (Ram Prasad) in favour of the name "Gujarmal," which he selected in honour of his step-mother.<ref>{{Cite web |title=:: MODI ENTERPRISES:: |url=https://www.modi.com/our-heritage.html |access-date=2026-07-30 |website=www.modi.com}}</ref>

During his time studying in the tenth standard, Gujarmal neglected to pay his examination fees, which resulted in the loss of an academic year. This incident led to his father inducting Gujarmal into the family business at a young age while simultaneously being home-schooled.{{sfn|Chauhan|1977|p=10–14}}

== Business career ==
In 1932, after a decade during which he grappled with personal issues and depression, Modi revived both his spirit and his business. After his second marriage that year, Modi became enthused and motivated for carrying on his business, because the sense of futility and depression left him when his wife became pregnant. Modi fulfilled his long-standing desire of expanding the family business to new sectors and territories. In 1932, with an amount of Rs. 400/-, he left for [[Delhi]] on the lookout for viable ventures.{{sfn|Chauhan|1977|p=28–32}} The village of Begumabad was finally selected as the site of his first independent venture— a sugar mill.{{sfn|Herdeck|Piramal|1985|p=237}} After initial difficulties in managing the sugar mill, Gujarmal successfully managed to turn things around to make his debut venture into a profitable entity. One of Gujarmal’s major successes was the toilet soap factory, which began operations in 1941. Gujarmal with the help of a Bengali gentleman figured out a way to produce toilet soap without the use of tallow— the substance used to make the soap cake dry and hard. Instead, his toilet soap factory used ''vanaspati'', from his ''vanaspati'' manufacturing unit, which proved to be a huge success.{{sfn|Chauhan|1977|p=46–48}}

==Personal life==
{{unsourced|section|date=April 2020}}
[[File:Gujarmal modi.jpg|thumbnail|right|Bust of Gujarmal Modi.]]
Modi was married aged twelve, in 1914, to a girl the same age as him. He and his wife therefore grew up together and were very attached to each other. Six years after their wedding, the couple became the parents of a child, but the newborn died within a few hours. Little did the family realize at that time that they were fated to relive this misery ten times over, for this heartbreaking event was to be tragically repeated that many times in as many years. During the years 1920-31, Modi's wife bore as many as ten children, but every single child died either in childbirth or in infancy. Medical care in semi-rural Begumabad was abysmal, and the Modi family was not yet seriously wealthy. Modi's wife also began keeping ill constantly, but it is not known whether this was a cause or a consequence of the loss of children. It became clear that further attempt at child-bearing would be both futile and dangerous to the health of the mother. Modi's wife despaired of motherhood, and joined family elders in counselling him to bring another wife home, saying that she would rejoice in his children, for they would be in some sense her own children.{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}}

Gujar Mal finally acceded to the entreaties of his father and first wife. Multani Mal set about searching for another suitable match, and on 19 June 1932, Gujar Mal was married to [[Dayawati Modi]], a lady of his own [[Marwari people|Marwadi]] community hailing from [[Etah district]] of Uttar Pradesh.{{sfn|Chauhan|1977|p=24}} Dayawati, the daughter of Chheda Lal, a tradesman of Etah, was seventeen years old; Gujar Mal was thirty. The two co-wives lived harmoniously together in the same household, because Gujar Mal began treating his first wife as a family elder. Dayawati was to become the mother of eleven healthy children, five sons and six daughters. Three daughters Rajkumari, Bimla and Rajeshwari were born before the birth of [[K K Modi]], their eldest son, in 1940. Their other sons are Vinay Kumar, Satish Kumar, [[Bhupendra Kumar Modi|Bhupendra Kumar]] aka Dr.M and Umesh Kumar.

==Personality==
Gujarmal was a staunch patriot and this was amply visible during his youth. In 1926, he was insulted on the basis of his nationality by an Englishman working in [[India]] by the name of Mr. Turner, after the young Modi outbid him during a public auction. An incensed Modi subjected the Englishman to a beating, which later resulted in a telling off by the Maharaja of Patiala; but earned him the respect of the public.{{sfn|Chauhan|1977|p=20–23}}

In 1945, after the end of the [[Second World War]], the British government wanted to confer a [[knighthood]] on Gujarmal for the exemplary service provided by his companies during the War. Gujarmal instead requested the British to confer on him an Indian title. The British duly complied and decided to honour him with the title of ''Raja Bahadur'', which was the catalyst behind the renaming of Begumabad to [[Modinagar]]. In 1946, the interim government of India decided to stop conferring titles and the decision to honour Gujarmal was deferred.{{sfn|Chauhan|1977|p=50–52}}

==Modi Group==
[[File:Modi at IPL Players Auction.jpg|thumb|left|Lalit Modi.]]
The [[Modi Group]] split in 1989, and the business was divided between the five sons of Gujarmal Modi, including [[Krishan Kumar Modi]], VK Modi, SK Modi, [[B. K. Modi]] and UK Modi and the three sons of his step brother Kedar Nath Modi. Krishan Kumar Modi, Gujarmal Modi's eldest son, owns Godfrey Phillips, the tobacco manufacturing company.<ref name=mo>{{cite news|url=http://businesstoday.intoday.in/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=13993&Itemid=1&issueid=78&sectionid=5&limit=1&limitstart=1|title=The empire crawls back |date=15 February 2010|publisher=Business Today}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.business-standard.com/india/news/bhupesh-bhandari-sparethought-for-lalit%5Cs-surname/392732/|title=Bhupesh Bhandari: Spare a thought for Lalit's surname|date=23 April 2010|publisher=Business Standard}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Modis erase rubber flagship|url=http://archive.tehelka.com/story_main9.asp?filename=Ne122504modies_erase.asp|publisher=Tehelka|access-date=24 January 2014}}</ref>

His brother K. N. Modi, died in 2005, at the age of 84. His son M.K. Modi is the head of Modipon Fibre, of the K.N. Modi Group, while his other son Y.K. Modi was FICCI president for many years.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.hindu.com/2005/05/29/stories/2005052902091200.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060519110715/http://www.hindu.com/2005/05/29/stories/2005052902091200.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=19 May 2006|work=[[The Hindu]]|title=Industrialist K.N. Modi passes away |date=29 May 2005}}</ref> Since the division, the Modi Group companies have underperformed and failed to match the successes achieved by the late Gujarmal Modi.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Rise, Fall & Rise of Indian Business Families|url=http://www.businessandeconomy.org/14122006/storyd.asp?sid=641&pageno=6|publisher=Business & Economy|access-date=31 January 2014}}</ref>

His son [[Krishan Kumar Modi]] and former chairman of Modi Group died at the age of 79 on 2 November 2019.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Th Indian Express |title=FICCI mourns demise of its former president K K Modi |url=https://indianexpress.com/article/business/business-others/industrialist-k-k-modi-dead-ficci-6101420/ |website=www.indiansexpress.com |date=3 November 2019 |publisher=The Indian Express}}</ref>

In April 2010, [[Krishan Kumar Modi]], had revealed that his eldest son [[Lalit Modi]] will succeed him as the helm of Modi Group's flagship business Godfrey Phillips India (GPI).<ref>{{cite news |last1=Mukherjee |first1=Shubham |title=Lalit will head family flagship, says father |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/Lalit-will-head-family-flagship-says-father/articleshow_new/5861586.cms?from=mdr |newspaper=The Times of India }}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
Modi had a telling impact on Indian commerce and industry and that is amply displayed by the awards and honours bestowed upon him. In 1968, he was decorated with the Padma Bhushan— the third-highest civilian award in India.<ref>{{cite web|title=Padma Bhushan |url=http://mha.nic.in/sites/upload_files/mha/files/LST-PDAWD-2013.pdf |publisher=Government of India |access-date=24 January 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151015193758/http://mha.nic.in/sites/upload_files/mha/files/LST-PDAWD-2013.pdf |archive-date=15 October 2015 }}</ref> The same year, he also became the President of the [[Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry]] (FICCI). Gujarmal held positions in various committees and business-governance bodies during his career.{{sfn|Chauhan|1977|p=72–79}}

*1960: Member of the Central Customs and Excise Advisory Committee
*1960: Vice-President of the Reserve Bank of Northern India
*1964: Member of the National Productivity Council
*1967: Member of the Export and Import Advisory Council & Indian Exports Organisation
*1968: Chairman of the International Arbitration Council

==Philanthropic activities==
GM Modi established various institutions in the fields of education, science, medicine and women’s welfare to uplift the country’s downtrodden and encourage competence-development in the youth. The Gujarmal Modi Innovative Science and Technology Award was instituted in 1988 in honour of his numerous philanthropic contributions to the field.<ref name=Philanthropy>{{cite news|title=Gujar Mal Modi Award for V.P. Sharma|url=http://www.thehindu.com/todays-paper/tp-national/tp-newdelhi/gujar-mal-modi-award-for-vp-sharma/article5008554.ece|work=The Hindu|date=9 August 2013 |access-date=24 January 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Gujar Mal Modi award for scientist Vinod Prakash Sharma|url=http://www.business-standard.com/article/pti-stories/gujar-mal-modi-award-for-scientist-vinod-prakash-sharma-113080900899_1.html|publisher=Business Standard|access-date=24 January 2014}}</ref>
